title: Recover Better: 10 Rules For Optimal Ultramarathon Recovery (iRunFar, 2014-09-09)
population: Coach and physical therapist guidance for ultramarathon recovery
findings: Rule 2: one day off running for every 10 miles raced (credited on the page to Pam Smith); for a heavy-vertical or high-altitude race, one day off for every 10 kilometres raced. Derived, not stated: 100 miles gives about 10 days by the miles rule, about 16 days by the km rule, and 50 km (about 31 miles) about 3 days.
Rule 3: commit to rest and recovery for a finite period of time, fixed in advance.
Rule 6: sleep one extra hour per night for every 10 miles raced, and for at least 10 days after a 100-mile race (as summarised on the page).

Rule 9: have the stride checked before resuming. Rule 10: start easy and slow; Pam Smith is quoted suggesting reversing taper mileage without the speed work, i.e. rebuilding weekly mileage before speed work.
limitations: One practitioner's rule of thumb quoted from another coach; derived day counts for 50 km and 100 miles are the reader's arithmetic, not on the page; no data cited; the Rule 6 wording is ambiguous in the summary fetched.
implications: A distance-scaled hold rule exists in convention: about 10 days (miles rule) or about 16 days (km rule, hilly) off after a 100-mile race, about 3 days after 50 km, which is a useful comparator for the engine's own holds.
The return shape is the reverse of a taper, easy, no speed, mileage before intensity; consistent with the engine's low-intensity return.

verification.notes: Re-fetched the page twice (WebFetch): author Joe Uhan, 'September 9, 2014'; rules 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10 and the Pam Smith attributions confirmed. Derived day counts kept and marked derived. Rule 6 sleep wording flagged as ambiguous. Practice source (programme, coaching or clinical page): a published convention, not evidence; grade D.

interests: Owns Uhan Performance Physiotherapy and offers online coaching (iRunFar bio); the day-off rule is credited to Pam Smith.

r1.note: Rules 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10 and the Pam Smith attributions located on the page fetched 2026-10-31 (published 2014-09-09, modified 2021-12-24); the day counts for 50 km and 100 miles are derived, as the record states.

r2.note: Author named (Joe Uhan). Western States' official 2012 results (read 2026-10-31) list Joe Uhan of Eugene OR in 9th place in 16:13:14; his doctorate in physical therapy and USATF Level II coaching rest on the iRunFar bio only. Interests recorded.

r3.note: Published 2014-09-09, modified 2021-12-24; the version read is the current page. Later corpus papers (hoffman-2017, garciavaliente-2026) describe recovery of function over days to weeks and do not supersede a days-off rule.

r4.note: A day off per 10 miles raced agrees in direction with Torrence (irunfar-2023: two to three weeks) and Roche (skurka-2017: a staged month) for a 100-mile effort, and hoffman-2017 and millet-2011 show function back by days 5 to 16. Roche's complete-rest week is shorter than Uhan's ten days; the conservative reading is the longer.

r5.note: Population is ultramarathoners after hard races, with the rule stated per miles raced; the H12 notes label the class mapping as derived.

r6.note: Evidence level D, at the practice cap.
